I am 45 years old and have been farming in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. My family has about 12 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know this soil well. I finished middle school, so I can read seed labels and follow extension recommendations, but I am not one to gamble with new crops I do not trust.

This year, I will stick to what works: **winter wheat followed by summer maize** on all 12 mu. That is the rotation everyone here relies on. The wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. In March I will top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up, and I will irrigate three times—once at jointing, once at heading, and once at grain filling if the spring is dry. I use improved wheat seed varieties that the local ag-supply shop recommends; they are not the most expensive hybrids, but they give me a stable 500 jin per mu and the grain buyer always takes them. I rotary-till before sowing wheat to break up the corn stubble.

After wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize with a no-till seeder. There is no time to waste between crops, and the soil holds enough moisture from the wheat season. I buy hybrid maize seed—usually something like Nongda 372—because the hybrid vigor is obvious; even with only two irrigations and less fertilizer than the wheat, I get 550 jin per mu or better. I spray herbicide and insecticide three times on the maize to control armyworm and weeds. I apply compound fertilizer at maize sowing and that is usually enough; the crop does not need as much fuss as wheat.

I thought about planting a couple of mu of cotton like some neighbors do, but cotton needs more than a dozen pesticide sprays and hiring pickers is expensive now. Wheat and maize have secure markets, the co-op buys them at guaranteed prices, and I can manage almost all the work myself with my small tractor. That is why I will put all my land into the wheat-maize rotation this year.
